summary:
APPA (Astronaut Physiological Prediction & Assistance) is a health‑monitoring platform that helps astronauts during space missions. APPA watches heart rate, ECG, blood pressure, blood glucose and oxygen saturation using sensors and medical devices that are connected. The data for APPA come from NASA sources such as CIPHER, other spaceflight experiments and synthetic mission profiles that fill in missing long‑term data. APPA contains a model that looks for possible presyncope events at 1 3, 5 and 10 minute timescales. It also has a case‑based system that finds similar physiological patterns. The dashboard lets users see health records, track measurements and capture readings from a camera, for the prototype. APPA also gives sleep schedules, nutrition ideas and exercise plans that match each crew member and mission phase. 

APPA is designed to raise health awareness spot risks early and keep astronauts safe during space exploration.
details:
APPA Astronaut Physiological Prediction & Assistance APPA is a comprehensive health-monitoring and assistance system to monitor astronauts' physiological changes during spaceflight and detect health risks before they become issues to help astronauts maintain their health and performance. It includes three integrated components, a physiological monitoring system, a machine-learning prediction model, and an interactive health-management website.

Physiological measurements recorded by the device include heart rate, electrocardiogram (ECG) signals, blood pressure, blood glucose and blood oxygen saturation (SpO). They are combined into a cohesive health profile that can be used to monitor the changes in an astronaut's physiologic state over time. By detecting the physiological signatures and estimating the probability that a presyncope event will happen in 1 3 5 and 10 minutes, the machine learning model will help establish when abnormal measurements occur and, more importantly, identify early signals that may lead up to the abnormal event.

Research Data and Scientific References

One of the primary difficulties encountered during the development of APPA was the scarcity of comprehensive astronaut physiological data, in particular continuous individual measurements spanning various phases of long-duration space missions.

To overcome this difficulty we referenced NASA approved studies and physiological experiments like: the Complement of Integrated Protocols for Human Exploration Research (CIPHER), Spaceflight Standard Measures, EDOMP, and more spaceflight studies. These studies gave us sources of reference, about physiology while in space and the impact of various stages of the mission on the human body.

We analyzed additional sets of physiological data, all acquired intending to providing insight on cardiovascular responses and orthostatic stress, and on the statistical links among physiological signals: NEGRAR, PhysioNet's Physiologic Response to Changes in Posture database. Data from spaceflight studies and complementary physiological experiments led to the formation of a scientific basis for this project's data analysis and machine-learning development.

The distinction made is between data presented in real scientific investigations and data modeled under experimental conditions. This is essential since the system represents an experimental research prototype and does not claim to be an astronaut medical history.

Machine-Learning Model

We have built an experimental machine-learning prediction system (based on Python/Scikit-learn). Our current implementation based on the HistGradientBoostingClassifier fits the data using these indices: physiological features (heart-rate metrics, PPG-derived pulse variability indicators, pulse-amplitude based features), contextual features (activity posture duration in upright position).

The output of the model is predections for four time horizons 1 3, 5 and 10 minutes. To enable a more robust assessment, the data was split by subject into a training, validation, and test set, with subjects being in only one of the groups. Model performance was assessed by calculating the precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, and Brier score.

This method enables us to explore the ability to detect pre-syncope physiological changes. Still, the present system is still an experimental research tool and additional validation with independent real-world physiological recordings is required before it can be used clinically or operationally.

Hardware and Physiological Monitoring

For the prototype physical demo, we chose three commercially available medical measurement devices: a digital blood pressure monitor, a blood-glucose measuring device (glucometer), and a pulse oximeter. These devices provide blood-pressure, blood-glucose, oxygen saturation, and pulse-rate measurements.

To hook these devices up to the website, we created a camera-based capture workflow. It takes pictures of the medical device's screen, pulls numerical values using optical character recognition (OCR), then shows a visualized list of retrieved values that the astronaut can confirm before entering onto his or her health dashboard.

In the subsequent development phase, we created a smaller design for this wireless wearable. It adds the MAX30102 optical PPG sensor for monitoring heart-rate and oxygen-saturation, the MAX30003 ECG analog front end for capturing electrical signals from the heart and to determine the R-R interval, and the BMI270 accelerometer and gyroscope to track motion and posture. All the components are designed to communicate via the nRF52840 low-power microcontroller using BLE.

A further future development proposed here, due to form an integral part of the architecture, is a CGM sensor like FreeStyle Libre and a small cuff-less wireless blood pressure monitor. Cuff-less blood pressure estimation using ECGPPG signals is a distinct research challenge and is envisaged as a subsequent development. These wearable items have yet to be integrated or even fabricated.

Website and Software Development

We developed a responsive web application called APPA Astronaut Health Companion, which serves as the central interface for the entire system. The website integrates physiological monitoring, health records, and daily wellness management into one accessible platform.

The Health Dashboard shows heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, oxygen saturation, measurement history and physiological trends. Camera Station gives camera-captured medical device, optical character recognition (OCR) extraction, and manual verification of readings. Crew Health Profile allows astronauts to input personal health data like height, body mass, existing health conditions medications allergies, dietary preferences, and activity restrictions.

It includes Sleep Management to administer sleep schedules and circadian rhythms, a Nutrition Planner to recommend menu options for mission phases, nutritional requirements, food types, storage constraints and crew preferences, as well as an Exercise Planner to categorize aerobic, resistive, and mobility exercise templates.

The Mission Log same thing arranges health data, sleep information and daily activities in a timeline, with Device Integration laying out the envisaged wearable tech and how it'll be wirelessly connected in time to the rest of the platform. A unified portal for viewing health data and scheduling daily wellness routines would be provided to spacefarers.

Tools, Programming Languages, and Technologies

APPA was built with multiple languages, libraries, and technologies. For the data processing analysis training, and evaluation of models, Python was used. HTML was used for the website's structure, CSS for styling and for the ability to dynamically resize the interface, and JavaScript for website interactivity, camera access, and OCR integration.

The Python development used NumPy to support numerical operations, Pandas to load and analyze data, Scikit-learn for code involving machine-learning development and evaluation, Matplotlib for the visualizations and evaluation plots, and Joblib to load and save trained models.

Other technologies involved Julius as the Python execution environment, project-file management, and website publishing platform; Tesseract.js for optimal character recognition within the browser; the Browser MediaDevices API to access the camera and capture images; and Bluetooth Low Energy architecture for the intended wireless sensor communication.

Creativity, Benefits, and Intended Impact

The innovative feature of APPA is that it combines physiologic monitoring, predictive modeling and daily health management for astronauts in a single package. The heart monitoring, glucose readings nutrition sleep and physical activity are no longer disparate activities, but are now part of one mission-oriented package.

Yet another element includes the integrated use of scientific discoveries based on spaceflight studies and a machine-learning prediction method for considering early physiological shifts related to presyncope risks. The website supports this method by making it easier to access, browse, and visualize physiological data, monitor shifts and structure daily data.

During the development of our prototypes, we discussed potential problems that could arise during space flight: microgravity physiological changes, orthostatic stress over gravity transitions, physiological variation, length of mission sensors measurement reliability, battery use comfort storage of food, and crew time restrictions.

To that end, APPA hopes to help astronaut safety and wellness, by assisting continuous health awareness, earlier detection of trends that may be about, and more efficient management of sleep, nutrition, exercise, and health observation across the duration of space missions.
